title: Life Found on Exoplanet? James Webb’s Stunning Discovery Explained
description:
Have we finally found life on another planet? The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has detected carbon dioxide, methane, and possibly dimethyl sulphide (DMS) in the atmosphere of the exoplanet K2-18b—a potential biomarker that, on Earth, is produced mostly by phytoplankton. Located 124 light years away in the constellation Leo, this mini-Neptune or possible Hycean World lies in the habitable zone of its red dwarf star, raising hopes for oceans and maybe even alien life.

Discovered by Kepler in 2015, K2-18b is 8.6 times the size of Earth. Earlier, Hubble Space Telescope confirmed water vapour in its atmosphere. Now JWST’s infrared data shows stronger evidence of carbon-based molecules, sparking excitement across the world. But is this really life—or just chemistry we don’t yet understand? In this video, we explain what scientists mean by biomarkers, how JWST’s transit method and spectroscopy work, why DMS is significant, and why we must wait for more data before making bold claims.

This is not “Earth 2.0” yet, but it is one of the strongest candidates for an Earth-like exoplanet with liquid water. As JWST prepares further observations with its MIRI instrument, we may soon know if K2-18b really harbours oceans and microscopic life. Stay tuned as we explore whether this is the first evidence of extraterrestrial life or just hype fueled by headlines.

#Exoplanet #JamesWebb #AlienLife #palebluethoughts
